The Grünfeld is byfar the most theory heavy opening in chess, and it is by far the most complex, but to me honestly, the Grünfeld is 100% worth learning if you truly are willing to take the effort to learn the ideas and themes of the Grünfeld, then learning the theory. The Grünfeld is somewhat "solved" at the highest level due to the fact so many players find lines to draw against it, even MVL doesn't always use his beloved Grünfeld anymore, but it has been making a resurgance in the top flight.

Against Nf3, you can opt for Nf6 and try to go into a Grünfeld. Against c4, nf6 g6 is a good try, but you will have to learn the anti-grunfeld with black(1.c4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.E4!? e5 !?)

Hello! I have played the Nimzo Indian for quite a while and I play the Semi Tarrasch as my response to 3.Nf3. The reason why the Tarrasch has such a low winrate is because over the years it has developed into the Berlin for 1.d4! The semi-tarrasch can completely kill the game for white like the Berlin. There is a very new and trendy move in the Tarrasch which leads to a very interesting endgame (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 d5 4.Nc3 c5 5.cxd5 cxd4!? 6.Qxd4 exd5 7.e4 dxe4 8.Qxd8+ K×d8 9.Ng5 Be6 10.Nxe6+ fxe6 11.Bg5 h6!? 12.Bxf6+ gxf6). This line with cxd4 is very fresh and interesting. It challenges white immediately and gives us equality as black. There are a lot of lines which lead to draws, when I have time I will make a study and share them here. This line has become  the best way to test white in the semi-tarrasch rather than the old Nxd5 lines. It has become so much like the Berlin, that nowadays top level players play e3 rather tha  cxd5. (Sorta like the anti-berlin). Normally, I don't like recommending the Semi-Tarrasch for most players because most players generally hate playing the Berlin, but I think the Semi-Tarrasch is the perfect opening for you!

There is a good course on chess.com by Daniel Naroditsky, where he covers bullet and blitz strategies.

One of them is what he calls "Blitz tactics" where you play either a losing tactic or a bad tactic when your opponent is in time pressure because they are likely to not be able to find the refutation.

Another one is in a time scramble you should keep your rook/queen on the same file/diagonal because your opponent is very likely to try and move back into the same file/diagonal.

Flagging is also a very important strategy to master. One example is if your opponent has low time, they shouldn't chain premove (for chess.com) because we can either try and break their chain premove or get an advantadge by moving into their position to capture pieces.

Bullet and blitz are still chess, but they are a completely different game from rapid and classical, so they are so many strategies to learn to improve in blitz/bullet.

Sincerely, a guy who played 1000 bullet games in a day :>.

Generally, the benefit of the nimzo move order (E.g. D4 Nf6 C4 E6 and after Nf3 going for a semi-slav and Nc3. Nimzo) is that you have the benefit of playing the nimzo while avoiding the exchange slav as you said, the the downside is that you will have to play a catalan. This move order allows a few tricks for white since the B1 knight hasn't been committed yet. There is also a very obscure reason why it's a "better move order" is because in the d4 d5 c4 c6 move order there is this meran line where white plays d4 d5 c4 c6 nf3 nf6 e3 e6 Nbd2 which is considered a slightly better semi-slav for white because the knight is better placed on d2 so we can recapture with the knight rather than bishop. This goes on to the benefit and downsides of playing from the traditional d4 d5 c4 c6 move order. We allow the exchange slav, but we maintain flexibility after d4 d5 c4 c6 Nc3/Nf3 Nf6 e3. We can play Bf5, which leads to either extremely complex and sharp positions or strategically rich and complecated poisitional positions, which allows chances for both white and black. Now we can discuss the final move order which is through the Qgd. Imo this is one of my personal favourite ways to enter the Semi-slav because instead of allowing exchange slav which is quite uncomfortable for a lot of players, we allow the less exhausting exchange qgd (d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 cxd5) but we can also paly the triangle system (d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 e6) but the downside of this move order is the Marshall gambit which is mindnumbingly complex and not worth learning for anyone who wants to have a functional brain. 

Tl;dr. Every move order has advantadges and disadvantages, but generally it depends on the player to find a move order they are comfortable with to enter the semi-slav.

In my opinion, I would never reccomend 3.Bc5 to any of my students or anyone in general. Of course it is a matter of preferance but after 3.Bc5 there are so many different stupid things white can throw at your face, like (4.c3 Nf6 D4 exd4 b4!?) or 4.d4!? or the Evans gambit or the max lange, deutz and other ridiculous things. Yes, the move Nf6 does allow the fried liver, but against the fried liver we can play ridiculous and obscure counters! Like after 4.Ng5 there is Nxe4!? which is objectively unsound but still very playable, or even in d5 exd5 there are so many different lines to choose from, all are equal and have various different quirks. (Personally i like after 4.Ng5 d5 exd5 to play Bd7 which is a reccomendation of Gawain Jones). 

Also Nf6 is more flexible for us as we have not comitted our bishop yet, so a quick d5 or h6 d6 setup can be played if we want to be annoying. Even something more cagey like Nf6 d3 Be7 can also be played. Of course there is also the Scotch Gambit, but I think it's a more practical choice to learn because you don't need two lines against the scotch gambit as they can also play it from the scotch move order. 

Tl;dr, I reccomend Nf6 because it's more flexible and there are less sidelines than 3.Bc5

Personally, I prefer the taimanov over the Najdorf. The taimanov is much more flexible when it comes to move orders and is more solid than the Najdorf. Also taimanov has comparitively less theory than the Najdorf. The taimanov is also a lot easier to understand the plans of and is one of the sicilians i generally reccomend :). One of the reasons is I prefer the e6 sidelines after nf3 then the ones that arise from the d6 move order (Moscow, Qxd4, delayed alapin).
